name: Fiske relational models theory

citation.title: The four elementary forms of sociality: Framework for a unified theory of social relations

summary: Relational models theory holds that people coordinate all social relationships using four elementary, innate-but-culturally-parameterized models (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching, market pricing); interactions outside these models are 'null' or asocial. Unit of analysis: the relationship/interaction between persons, which may combine models across domains. Also: Fiske, A. P. (1991). Structures of Social Life: The Four Elementary Forms of Human Relations. New York: Free Press.

constructs.label: Four elementary relational models
constructs.notes: Verified on the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry, which cites Fiske 1991 and 1992 with the same labels. Each model corresponds to a measurement scale type (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) per Fiske 1992 (KNOWLEDGE).

constructs.label: Null / asocial relation
constructs.notes: IEP: brute coercive manipulation is not Authority Ranking but the 'Null Relation', in which people treat each other in non-social ways. Fiske 1991/1992 also describe 'asocial' interaction (treating others as objects or nonentities).

verification_notes: Four model labels, the null relation, and both primary citations (1991 Free Press; 1992 Psych Review 99, 689-723) verified on IEP. Fiske's own UCLA relmodov page and the APA record were not reachable.

citation.title: What is emotional intelligence?
citation.venue: In P. Salovey & D. J. Sluyter (Eds.), Emotional Development and Emotional Intelligence: Educational Implications (pp. 3-31). Basic Books

summary: The ability model defines emotional intelligence as a set of cognitive abilities for processing emotional information, organized into four hierarchically arranged branches from basic perception to reflective regulation, and measured with performance (right/wrong) tasks in the MSCEIT. Unit of analysis: the individual's emotion-processing abilities. Also: Salovey, P., & Mayer, J. D. (1990). Emotional intelligence. Imagination, Cognition and Personality, 9(3), 185-211. doi:10.2190/DUGG-P24E-52WK-6CDG.

constructs.label: Four branches of emotional intelligence (Mayer & Salovey 1997)
values: Perceiving emotions (perception, appraisal, and expression of emotion)
Using emotions to facilitate thought (emotional facilitation of thinking)
Understanding emotions (understanding and analyzing emotions; employing emotional knowledge)
Managing emotions (reflective regulation of emotions to promote emotional and intellectual growth)
constructs.notes: Short labels: perceiving, using/facilitating, understanding, managing. Parenthetical text gives the 1997 chapter's longer branch headings from memory.

name: Goleman/Boyatzis emotional and social intelligence competency model (ESCI)

citation.title: Emotional intelligence has 12 elements. Which do you need to work on?

summary: Goleman's mixed/competency model treats emotional intelligence as a set of learned, behaviourally observable competencies that distinguish outstanding performers, organized into four domains; the current Goleman-Boyatzis model (operationalized in the Korn Ferry Emotional and Social Competency Inventory, ESCI) has 12 competencies. Unit of analysis: the individual's workplace/leadership competencies as rated by self and others. Also: Goleman, D. (1995). Emotional Intelligence. Bantam. Goleman, D. (1998). Working with Emotional Intelligence. Bantam. Boyatzis, R. E., & Goleman, D. (2007). Emotional and Social Competency Inventory. Hay Group (now Korn Ferry).

constructs.label: Four domains of EI
constructs.notes: Verified on Key Step Media (Goleman's publishing company). Often written 'Self-Awareness' and 'Self-Management' in HBR/ESCI materials.

name: Bar-On model of emotional-social intelligence (EQ-i)

citation.title: The Bar-On model of emotional-social intelligence (ESI)

summary: Bar-On defines emotional-social intelligence as a cross-section of interrelated emotional and social competencies, skills and facilitators that determine how effectively we understand and express ourselves, understand and relate to others, and cope with daily demands; it is operationalized by the 133-item self-report EQ-i (Bar-On 1997), yielding a total EQ score, 5 composite scale scores and 15 subscale scores. Unit of analysis: the individual's self-reported emotionally and socially intelligent behaviour. Also: Bar-On, R. (1997). The Emotional Quotient Inventory (EQ-i): Technical manual. Multi-Health Systems (Toronto).

constructs.label: EQ-i composite scales
constructs.notes: Verbatim from Bar-On 2006, p. 14 (primary PDF text extracted locally). A total EQ score sits above these.

constructs.label: EQ-i 15 subscales, grouped by composite
constructs.notes: Verbatim naming and grouping from Bar-On 2006, p. 14. The paper also mentions two validity indices (Positive Impression, Negative Impression) used as a correction factor.

verification_notes: Primary source fully verified: Psicothema HTML page gave the citation and scale list; the open-access PDF text (extracted locally with pypdf) confirmed the exact composite and subscale names and grouping on p. 14.
